summary: Allows DNSSEC-validating resolvers to use NSEC and NSEC3 records from cache to generate negative answers for whole ranges of names, and positive answers from wildcards. This can improve speed, reduce load, and increase privacy. It updates RFC 4035 and is updated by RFC 9077.

plainLanguage.summary: A validating DNS resolver can use a signed proof about a range of names to answer later queries from its cache. This avoids repeating some lookups, while requiring the resolver to validate the proof and limit how long it relies on it.

questions: how does dnssec negative caching work
what is the maximum negative cache ttl
subtitle: Let a validating DNS resolver answer from cached proofs about ranges of names.

tldr.problem: A DNS resolver normally needs an exact cached result, even when a signed denial already proves that a whole range of names does not exist. Repeating those lookups adds delay, server work, traffic, and privacy exposure.
tldr.mechanism: A DNSSEC-validating resolver uses cached NSEC or NSEC3 records to synthesize negative answers for names they cover. It can also use cached wildcard records to synthesize positive answers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 4035 and recommends limiting the effective negative-answer TTL to 10800 seconds. The unit metadata says RFC 8198 is updated by RFC 9077.

today: RFC 8198 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4035 and is updated by RFC 9077. It specifies aggressive use of DNSSEC-validated cache data.

sections.title: Why Exact-Match Caching Falls Short
sections.content:
A DNS negative cache remembers that a requested name or record type does not exist. In the usual exact-match model, a resolver that has learned one name is absent may still contact authoritative servers for another name covered by the same signed proof.

RFC 8198 lets DNSSEC-validating resolvers use cached NSEC and NSEC3 records to synthesize negative answers. It also permits positive answers based on cached wildcard records.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed denial can cover a range of names, but an ordinary negative cache may remember only the name asked about. This RFC lets a validating resolver reuse the wider proof.

sections.title: What a Cached Denial Proves
sections.content:
An NSEC record identifies names that appear before and after a gap in a signed DNS zone. A query name within that gap is proven not to exist. NSEC3 provides a related proof using hashed names.

Without aggressive use, a later query for another name in the same range can trigger another lookup. The RFC identifies the resulting costs as extra bandwidth and server work, longer waits, possible denial-of-service pressure, and disclosure of queries.
sections.plainLanguage: A validated NSEC or NSEC3 record can show that a queried name falls in a proven gap. The resolver can reuse that proof instead of asking the authoritative server again.

sections.title: When the Resolver Can Answer from Cache
sections.content:
If its negative cache contains enough information to validate an answer, a validating resolver SHOULD use cached NSEC, NSEC3, and wildcard records to synthesize a response. If the cache cannot prove the answer, the resolver MUST ask the authoritative servers as usual.

NSEC3 requires checks for empty non-terminals and wildcard cases. A covering NSEC3 record with the Opt-Out flag does not prove that the name is absent, so the resolver cannot use it for aggressive negative caching.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver answers from cache only when validated records prove the result. If it cannot establish that proof, it sends the query to the authoritative server.

sections.title: Using Cached Wildcard Records
sections.content:
A wildcard record can provide an answer for a name that is not explicitly listed in a zone. If a validating resolver can establish that the name would not exist without the wildcard match, it SHOULD synthesize the positive answer or NODATA response from the wildcard information in its cache.

If the wildcard record is not cached, the resolver MUST ask the authoritative servers. This rule covers positive answers as well as negative answers.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver can reuse a validated wildcard record when it proves that the wildcard applies to the queried name. If the record is not in cache, the resolver asks the authoritative server.

sections.title: TTL Limits and the RFC 4035 Update
sections.content:
RFC 8198 replaces the advice in RFC 4035 that resolvers avoid synthesizing responses from wildcard or NSEC data. Once records are validated, DNSSEC-enabled resolvers SHOULD use them until their effective TTLs or signatures expire.

New names may not become usable while cached negative information remains effective. The RFC RECOMMENDS that validating resolvers cap the effective TTL of negative responses at 10800 seconds and reduce NSEC or NSEC3 TTLs to SOA.MINIMUM when that value is smaller.
sections.plainLanguage: The updated rule lets resolvers use validated cached proofs until they expire. The RFC recommends a maximum effective negative-answer cache time of 10800 seconds.

sections.title: Validation and Cache-Poisoning Risk
sections.content:
A resolver must validate NSEC and NSEC3 records before using them this way; the RFC warns that unvalidated use can create serious security problems. A forged old denial could suppress queries for several new names when its proof is reused from cache.

Although a record's TTL is often shorter than its signature lifetime, the resolver can limit the exposure by capping effective negative TTLs. If an aggressive-caching algorithm fails, the resolver MUST fall back to ordinary resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: Only validated denial records are safe to reuse. A forged cached proof could affect several names, so resolvers should limit its lifetime and fall back to normal lookups if processing fails.
